Terrible link to plaid. The CoPilot app itself is solid. The interface is intuitive, the budgeting tools are thoughtfully designed, and the categorization engine is one of the few that actually learns user behavior instead of making a mess after every single transaction. If I were rating only CoPilot’s internal functionality, it would easily be a five-star product. The problem is everything that sits between CoPilot and the banks it needs to talk to.

Navy Federal and the Plaid integration are, frankly, hot garbage. Nothing connects correctly, nothing stays synced, and the error messages are so vague that you end up wasting time troubleshooting problems the app can’t fix because the underlying data link simply doesn’t work. Every attempt to authenticate with Navy Federal through Plaid turns into a full-scale exercise in frustration, circular prompts, and outright failure. When the main value of a budgeting app depends on accurate account aggregation, having your primary financial institution break the entire workflow is unacceptable.

What makes this even more frustrating is that CoPilot could be outstanding—its design is genuinely strong. But none of that matters if the connectivity layer collapses every single time. When your bank accounts won’t stay linked and half the transactions never load, you’re left with an expensive app that functions worse than a notebook. At this point, using graph paper would be more reliable than dealing with this dysfunctional chain of broken connections.

CoPilot deserves credit for what it controls, but Navy Fed and Plaid drag the experience down so far that the usefulness of the app is severely compromised. Until those two decide to operate at even a minimally functional level, CoPilot’s potential is wasted.

The best.  THE BEST.. I have used several personal finance apps over the years. Copilot is the best for two big reasons.

First, the desktop app is so fast and nimble that I was able to, over the course of a few hours,  review a couple years of past transactions so I could accurately identify spending patterns and -- more importantly-- winkle out all those surprise recurring transactions.  I cancelled about a dozen forgotten quarterly and annual charges -- paying for the cost of copilot  ten times over.

Secondly, once I had the true list of recurring transactions, copilot does the best job in incorporating those anticipated costs into my monthly spending.  It includes all those costs at the top of the month so I know exactly how much discretionary money I actually have to spend.  It also shows recurring costs in each category in a neat visual so I can really see how much margin I have for day to day expenses.  I can actually check to see where I'm at during the month before I buy something.

Now, I look forward to checking the app every day because using Copilot gives me a wonderful sense of clarity and control I've never had with any other personal finance app. ❤️❤️❤️💵💵💵

Excellent, life changing. But, needs refinement. Copilot is an excellent app that more than deserves 5 stars. I’ve been using the app since 2021, and have gotten 8 people to start using it. I believe that it can make a huge difference if you are ready to commit to smarter financial habits. The app is beautifully designed which gamifies your personal finances and makes something most people find dreadful to be fun, exciting, and even additive.

As a longtime user, I do have several feature requests that I believe could improve and refine this great app. Some of these are cosmetic and others are seriously annoying things that they really should fix.

1. Please please fix graphs. When you have a category that you used to spend a lot in but now spend a lot less, the bars are barely visible. The bars should scale according to the local max on the screen and not the global max which is potentially from years ago. This can render the graph completely useless. The graphs in investing and accounts also need a refresh. I don’t find them useful as they are too small! Give us better graphs and just data visualization in general. 
2. Rules absolutely NEED a redesign like yesterday. The fact you can’t manage your rules at this point is insane. Second, please let us create a rule without needing to apply it to every transaction it finds ever. I have years of specific categorization that I don’t necessarily want to mass change just to set a rule. Just let us set a rule for future transactions only. This makes no sense 
3. We should be able to archive a category or hide it from view somehow but keep the totals in your numbers. I used to vape and I don’t need a vapes category anymore but also don’t want to just delete all the spending or put it into miscellaneous. 
4. I would love to be able to group groups. For example I have my car group and also another transportation group that has public and ride share. I’d love to be able to group these 2 so I can know how much I’m spending on transportation total, but also be able to drill down into how much I spend on my car. Adding Ubers to my car group would not let me see just how much I spend on my car but also I have to sum 2 groups to know my transportation spend.
Anyway keep killing it copilot team. I’ve seen yall release some bangers so I have faith this app will only get better. Also please don’t forget us users with a ton of data, I have been through periods where performance has suffered very badly but yall have fixed it so please don’t stop addressing that.

Beautiful app, but progress on missing features is slow. This is a gorgeous, Apple-native finance app that’s full of clever features and design decisions. I like so much of it that I want to use it for my bookkeeping, but a number of issues prevent that. First, it’s wild that you cannot see or edit any rules you make for categorizing your expenses. I know you can contact support and they’ll delete a rule for you, but the fact that this has remained an issue for years makes me question priorities. 

I need a way of marking charges as shared/split (and specifically, rules to do this automatically…), which ultimately makes it impossible for me to actually track my budget with this app. I know this isn’t the most common scenario, but it’s also not rare. 

The prioritization of things like Genmoji integration (cute!) or most recently a web app (useful!) to me feel less important than filling some of the missing features that actually let you control your budget. And the team is small enough that there’s maybe one major feature a year. That pace is fine once the foundation is there, but it feels like the app has a lot of low hanging fruit that may take years to get to. 

Again, I want to use this app — it’s so much nicer than a homegrown Google Sheet or any of the other big apps! But if it doesn’t currently fully match your needs, it probably won’t for a long time.

The Feature that keeps me Subscribed. I love Copilot for one feature in particular. When you go out to dinner with friends and pay the bill, then get paid back through Venmo, Apple Cash, or Zelle, Copilot makes it easy to track your true spending.

For example, if the bill is $200 but your portion was only $50, you can categorize the incoming payments (Friends Venmo’s) under the restaurant category. Copilot subtracts those reimbursements, so it only shows that you spent $50 that month.

You can do this for anything—group dinners, movies, or golf. It makes seeing exactly what you’re spending each month incredibly easy

Other, less-pressing problems (for me) have to do with look-and-feel issues, and so are completely subjective.

Navigating to text fields within the app has never felt intuitive. 

Year-end summary does not allow me to page to whichever category I want to see - I can only move forward-back one page at a time in the order Copilot has arranged for me. If you’re going to include a “feature,” fine, but design it in a way that anticipates users wanting to do more with it than just passively follow the directions onscreen.

Again, for the price, this app is a solid choice for tracking and organizing finances. But it could be so much more if the designers made up their minds to do a better job of meeting the needs and expectations of their users.

So Close To Being Really Good. I really wanted to use Copilot and tried to make it work, but there were too many little annoyances that finally made me give up. 

One of them was having to manually create two transactions for things like my car payment. For whatever reason, Plaid couldn’t connect to my car loan account, so I had to manually add it. The rigamarole of having to create manual transactions to debit the money from my checking and the create another transaction to my car loan account to show the payment was time consuming, frustrating, and quite frankly unnecessary. Being able to transfer money from a payment account to a loan account should be one transaction.  I had three loan accounts I would have to do this for. 

I also found the iPad version of Copilot slow, sometimes unresponsive, unintuitive, and quite inferior to the iPhone app.  Things in the iPad app did not work the same and were missing features. For example, when entering a manual internal transfer, the “incoming” or “outgoing” selector buttons were not available. Sometimes clicking on a field would bring up a numeric keypad while other times in would bring up a full keyboard. 

Finally, Copilot relies heavily on Plaid for connecting to banks. Unfortunately, this system was much less reliable than what I found in other finance apps. 

I would be willing to give Copilot another shot once they are able to update the iPad app and fix a lot of these issues.

From 5 to 3 stars. I love the interface because it’s colorful and easy to navigate. It’s so easy to categorize transactions and see where all of your money is. The rollover feature is perfect for me rather than having to track individual sinking funds. It didn’t take long to set up at all, and it shows me everything I need without having to run reports or search for it, such as the average amount I’m spending per category per month, which updates automatically. I’m switching from YNAB, and I hated the give every dollar a job model. In Copilot Money, you don’t have to move assigned dollars between categories every time money moves between your accounts. This app has given me the flexibility I need in my budget while still maintaining control over my finances. My one suggestion is to add an auto-distribute function for splitting transactions so I don’t have to manually calculate sales tax for each category.

EDIT: I have canceled my free trial and will be going back to spreadsheets. So far the customer support has been good. One of my accounts will not connect and they have been working diligently to resolve the issue - much appreciated. However, I discovered that a bunch of my transactions are missing. Initially, when I connected my accounts, it imported 2 1/2 years worth of data. I had to manually delete everything prior to this year, which was difficult because I kept trying to delete things and they wouldn’t disappear so I had to do it repeatedly. Now I’m discovering that most of my categories are missing transactions between January and April 2026. I tried entering them manually but it’s a bit tedious. I can’t customize the color of the accounts and when I search for them, the font is too small so it’s difficult to find the one I’m looking for plus they always come up in a different order. I also don’t like that I cannot re-order my categories or my recurrings. Speaking of recurrings, the app is not recognizing new transactions, even though I have set up a rule for the name. Some of my recurrings are duplicated and I can’t rename them. Visually the list is a mess. In addition, I have to agree with other users that there is no easy way to see what is available to spend. I find myself toggling back-and-forth between the cash flow tab, the dashboard and my categories but still not feeling certain about the information it’s giving me. Yesterday I was reviewing new transactions and one of them was categorized incorrectly even though I have at least five other transactions from the same place. When I re-categorized it, I found that all the previous transactions were also categorized incorrectly, even though I’ve already gone through every single transaction in my history and made sure that it was right. Somehow it got changed? I really like the layout of this app and at first it seemed great but now I’m finding too many functional errors.

Whenever you log a transaction against the fund, it updates the balance as expected (positive or negative). But It also updates the total remaining amount to spend for the entire monthly budget, and it drives me bonkers! For example, if I log an unexpected $1000 charge against my emergency fund (25k total), that fund will be updated to $24k but the monthly budget will say I’m $1k overbudget. Same thing if I have an unexpected windfall of $5000 that I add to the fund; it’ll say I have $5000 more to spend for that month. It can make it really confusing because I just want a snapshot of how I’m doing for the month excluding extraneous transactions. I just wish it would keep funds separate. I just log my savings as a line item and then do the funds in a spreadsheet because it’s so frustrating, Some additional graphs in the free tier would be a nice update too. (And it seems to be available in other free apps). For example, you can see the pie chart split by category for the current month (housing, lifestyle, etc) but you currently can’t scroll back to previous months. I can’t say if there are more features with the paid version, but these elements stood out to me.

Great concept, but app needs work. I’m very grateful for this app, and at the same time I have various qualms with its many quirks, which are numerous enough that on the daily I tend to ask myself if it would be easier to write myself an Excel sheet for this purpose. And I pay for premium.

For example: the default view of this app should not be the “today” page. This is a learning summary page. It should be in the back of the deck where I can access it when I want to learn or view summaries. In fact, you should probably just get rid of it all together, since you have other tabs dedicated for those purposes.

The most useful page on this app, to be used on the daily, is the budget section. A most common use case is for me to want to buy something… Not know how much I have left in my envelope for that thing… And eopening my app in order to get answers. That is what prevents overspending. Instant information sharing. Not Some page doggedly trying to get me to use the tutorial system.

This brings me to my second criticism: why do the pages not seem to speak to each other consistently? If I’ve created dozens of budgets in this app, why am I still being asked to “get started on my first budget”? There does not seem to be any manual way to correct this misinformation. I simply must go through the tutorial in order to get rid of that call to action. so now, not only do I have an annoying default page that I have to scroll past in order to get to relevant information, but the information it’s giving me isn’t even valid. 




third, and this is a big one: assigning transactions to envelopes takes way too long. Here is the process: 1. Click transaction. 2. Visually find the small, nondescript section that allows you to assign it to an envelope. Click that. 3. Click the search bar. (Because nobody wants to visually scroll past dozens of fund titles, guys). 4. Search for the right envelope. click it. 5. Press done. to go back to the data page. 6. Press done AGAIN to fully assign the transaction. 

I understand that you created the fast track function to try to make this better. But let’s be real, it’s only correct about 30% of the time. And in a world where we can simply swipe left or right to find a love match, I simply must believe that there is a faster way to getting this tedious process done. Here’s a suggestion that won’t require a complete architectural rewrite:

1. Click on transaction. If we must default to the transaction data page, fine, but the search bar is on that page. Furthermore, the search bar is immediately in focus, allowing us to 
2. Instantly start typing the name of the fund. Similar to Excel‘s filter function, funds that are caught by the search are instantly selected.
3. Big, noticeable, DONE button. Not some tiny white font up in the corner.

That’s it. onto the next transaction. 

There is so much needless stuff shoved onto this transaction data page that could be moved to a second page. you need some of it to remember what the transaction was about. But…a “share transaction” button?? Big and bold, where the “DONE” button probably should be? while the “done” button gets shoved into the tiny upper-right corner? a check# section? even notes are unnecessary at this stage. You’re trying to be helpful, but at the cost of slowing down a daily, predictable, repeatable process that you’re also asking everybody to invest in as a habit. In other words, it’s bad design to code for the exceptions rather than the most common use case.

there’s additional stuff… bank transactions still take way too long to show up, funds are clunky to work with, the app consistently signs me out… for reasons unknown to me… every couple of days I need to sign back in…

Like I said. I’m grateful for it, but it needs work, and I’d love to see some of these essential, time-eating design flaws getting addressed, rather than a new dark mode.

Overall great app, I’d like to suggest a key adjustment:. I really enjoy the app, however I am a strong believer in the saying “garbage in - garbage out” when it comes to providing relevant data. Specifically, I see an area where I believe we can fine tune data input in order to get better data output, thus, giving the user a better experience. For instance, when using “Paycheck Planning” the current feature splits a bi-weekly paycheck right down the middle at 50%, I would like it to instead be adjustable for those of us who receive a larger paycheck at the end of the month compared to our first paycheck of the month. 

What might this look like? Picture this: Billy Bob is an hourly paid employee and makes $10,000 net each month. Billy Bob is paid bi-weekly, however, his last paycheck of the month factors the entire months “per diem” as well as any overtime hours. Let say 25% of the total $10,000 monthly paycheck is paid on the 3rd of the month, while the other 75% of his paycheck ($7,500) is paid on the 17th of the month. This isn’t currently factored into the Every Dollar app and can make budgeting difficult.

A nice NEW FEATURE to the Every Dollar app would be a sliding adjustable percentage widget, allowing the user to adjust what percentage of their Total Monthly Pay is paid through the 1st versus 2nd paycheck.

So for example, if I get my paycheck income on my checking account, I would have to attribute that income to my goal. But that’s not realistic because I would transfer that money to my savings account or my investment account. But you can’t link a transfer to a goal. You also can’t see transactions on investment accounts right now (it’s in beta but it doesn’t work). I also can’t make a rule for transfers accurately (they need to allow the rules to say “from account” and “to account” because just filtering “account” isn’t specific enough), nor can I set up my savings as an expense without having to manually input those expenses as a contribution to the goal. I hope this makes sense but basically TLDR transferring money is not a forte for this platform. I do like that it says transferring money doesn’t have to be tied to the budget so that’s helpful but I do wish there was some way to actually link the transfer information. I don’t want to think of a transfer from my checking to my credit card as an “expense” and then an “income”. It should just be a transfer that I can attribute to both accounts. Honestly, I’ve gotten rid of my goals because they just became too annoying to deal with and if you do a rule where you put a bunch of transactions linked to a goal, you cannot mass change it or revert it so you also have to manually fix it if you accidentally do that or just delete the goal. Basically what I am saying though is that saving money and tracking savings in your budget is not flushed out enough because now my savings I have to consider as an expense because I can’t accurately categorize transfers as a saving. If I could say “transfers from X account to Y account contribute to my goal” that would be great, but all it is is “transfers in X account”. I don’t want ALL of the transfers contributing to the goal. Sorry for the rant but it definitely is something that I think should be more fine tuned. Unless I am missing an entire functionality.

Not quite a Mint replacement. The original mint.com app and website won users over from Intuit Quicken in part from how it elegantly handled transfer transactions between accounts, such as credit card account payments from a checking account. In Aaron Patzer’s original product, this was automatic. Monarch, otoh, has to be trained to do this, account by account— and if the transfer transactions signatures change in the slightest, it forgets this training, and reverts to booking credit card payments received as income, and the corresponding checking account transactions as expenses, wrecking cash flow reporting. So I’m effectively back to Quicken 98 behavior, in 2026, with the added bonus that I pay annually for the privilege of having my financial data online to be mined. Reconsidering my options now.

Monarch Made Taxes & Biz Ops So Much Easier!. If you’re looking for a budgeting app that is the complete package, this is it - it has an elegant design (+1–orange is my fave too), a UX that is easy to navigate and customize, for both quick glance features and in-depth info with charts, filters, tags, colors, etc.

My personal fave features are the Recurring section where it lists all your monthly recurring income and expenses and shows you a calendar with dots on the days and notifies you in a few days in advance so you’re always prepared. 

The other is the Create Rule feature that allows you to take a transaction and customize it to automatically have attributes you assign for all future transactions. Say you have a business expense for supplies every few months that you want to tag (label) as business-related and/or as a tax write-off - any time you make this purchase in the future it will now have those tags. You can also edit the merchant name to better match what it reflects and much more. 

Lastly I recently had to fill out 6 months of profit & loss forms for legal purposes and I used the new AI they’ve implemented to automatically gather the items I specified, itemize them, and give me totals so I could simply plug-in the numbers (after double checking them for accuracy, of course 😉). 

I know there’s a number of good financial budgeting apps out there right now, but I’m glad I decided to try Monarch and it’s been so helpful with taxes and other legal uses that I’ve decided to keep subscribing at $14.99/month. 

At times, I wish it were a little cheaper, but when you consider the real-life implications of financial organization (or lack thereof) and how the practicality of an app like this changes the game for those things, the value you get in return is worth a lot more than $14.99 a month. 

Highly recommended app if you’re serious about your financial life.

Premium Price, Surprisingly Basic Problems. TL;DR: Monarch has some good ideas and is generally well designed, but for $15/month it gets several basic things wrong: the trial is too short, auto-categorization is unreliable, rule priority is opaque, and category/budget organization is unnecessarily confusing and restrictive.

Full Review:
Monarch is feature-rich and mostly well designed, but several fundamental blunders seriously degrade the experience and make me question how a $15/month, award-winning budgeting app can get some of the basics so wrong.

First, the 7-day free trial is far too short and feels greedy. This is a budgeting app built around monthly budgeting. You realistically need at least one full budgeting cycle to understand how transactions, rules, rollovers, recurring expenses, and actual spending behave over time. Seven days is barely enough to finish setting everything up, much less evaluate whether the product actually works for you.

Second, auto-categorization needs to be rock solid at this price, and it simply isn’t. Monarch categorized a Baskin-Robbins purchase as a coffee shop. Baskin-Robbins. One of the most recognizable ice cream chains in America. As a coffee shop. That is the budgeting-app equivalent of categorizing McDonald’s as a hot dog stand. Mistakes happen, sure, but errors this basic seriously undermine confidence in the system.

The rule system is unnecessarily opaque and inflexible. Rules apparently execute in top-to-bottom order, with the first overlapping rule winning, yet this hierarchy is not made clear in the UI. Worse, there is no way to reorder rules. If rule priority matters to the outcome, users need both a clear indication of that priority and direct control over it.

Category organization is another mess. Categories exist within groups, yet the settings UI presents groups and categories together in a flat list at essentially the same visual level, even though they are fundamentally different objects. Group ordering should be clearly separated from category ordering within each group. Reordering itself also seems buggy, with changes sometimes failing to persist, and it is unclear how the order configured there relates to the ordering shown in the Budget tab. This entire interaction needs a rethink.

Finally, Flexible budget items appear to be automatically ordered by spending level, with no obvious way to manually reorder the groups and categories. Why? A premium budgeting app should not be making an arbitrary presentation decision like this with no override. Fully unconstrained category and group ordering is a basic organizational feature, not an advanced request.

There is a lot to like about Monarch, which makes these shortcomings surprising and more frustrating. The app is close to being excellent, but at $15/month the standard should be much higher. Basic categorization accuracy, understandable rule precedence, reliable reordering, and full control over budget organization should already be solved problems.

Nearly perfect - love it - highly recommend. Overall, I love Monarch Money! It does an excellent job of connecting to almost all my financial accounts and has become an invaluable tool for understanding and managing my household finances.

One of its greatest strengths is the ability to track spending across multiple accounts in one place. Instead of reviewing individual bank accounts and credit card statements, I can see where our money is going, identify spending patterns, compare expenses from month to month, and distinguish recurring expenses from occasional purchases. This makes it much easier to understand our actual cost of living, identify opportunities to save, and make informed financial decisions. I particularly appreciate being able to examine individual transactions rather than relying solely on broad spending categories.

I also love the ability to download transactions as CSV files. This allows me to conduct more detailed analysis in Excel, create customized reports, and track spending over longer periods. An option to automate or schedule these exports would make an already excellent feature even better.

The new email receipt system is a fantastic improvement, especially for tracking Apple purchases and subscriptions. Being able to connect receipts to transactions makes it much easier to understand charges that otherwise appear with vague merchant descriptions.

There are, however, a few areas that could be improved.

Account connectivity: Reauthorizing accounts that require two-factor authentication can be frustrating. I wish there were an easier, centralized process for identifying disconnected accounts and reconnecting them.

Duplicate accounts: When a retirement account becomes disconnected and is subsequently reconnected, it can be difficult to determine whether Monarch has created a duplicate. This raises concerns about the accuracy of account balances and net worth calculations. Better duplicate detection and a straightforward way to reconcile accounts without losing transaction history would be extremely helpful.

Transfers versus income: Monarch could do a better job distinguishing actual income and expenses from transfers between accounts. Internal transfers, credit card payments, and certain retirement transactions can distort income and spending reports when they are incorrectly categorized. Better automatic identification and reconciliation would significantly improve the reliability of its financial reporting.

Despite these issues, Monarch is an excellent product. It has given me a much clearer picture of our household finances and made tracking spending considerably easier. I especially appreciate that it provides both an accessible overview of our finances and the flexibility to conduct more detailed analysis when I want to dig deeper.

TLDR - There are way better options, like Monarch.. When Mint went EOL, I, like many others, migrated to PocketGuard. I find budgeting very difficult and Mint worked extremely well for me. I read that PocketGuard was the most similar, and they have released updates that made it more similar. 

UNFORTUNATELY, PocketGuard has several fundamental flaws that make it so irritating to use that I stopped using it entirely and my finances suffered as a result. I’ll start with the good.

The good: you can set budgets and roll them over into the next month. This rollover feature was not an offering when I started using it, somehow. You can also now set rules to categorize transactions automatically which was not the case when I started using it; I initially had to recategorize every individual transaction if PocketGuard thought it belonged in a different budget. (This is still the case if the payment issuer name changes but I can’t really fault them for that.)

The bad: one of pocketguard’s selling points is its bill tracking feature. Unfortunately, this feature is actually a drawback, as whenever PocketGuard says something is a bill, it breaks it out from your budget entirely and does not let you set a monthly budget for it. This is fine for rent, but it is utterly broken for things like quarterly water bills, when the app says “scheduled for [month]” and does not count a portion of that quarterly or yearly bill towards your monthly budget. Instead, when you hit that month, suddenly you’re completely over budget because your entire quarterly water bill or annual Strava subscription or property tax is counted towards that month alone. Many times I tried to figure out a way to make this feature work for me, but it just does not. It is also a pain for the purpose of tracking things like streaming subscriptions, because even if you set an entertainment budget and categorize Spotify as entertainment, the app then DOUBLE COUNTS that recurring payment as a) a bill and b) part of your set entertainment budget. It also does not automatically deduct recurring payments such as these from your budget so that you can easily see the actual amount you have free to spend. Most of these issues have been immediately fixed for me by moving to Monarch instead. I only wish I had done so before my annual PocketGuard subscription had pinged.

Cash transactions. The app is very helpful overall, but one major limitation affects real-world use: cash transactions cannot be closed automatically within a series unless they’re linked to a digital payment.

In many everyday situations, cash is still the only acceptable form of payment. For example, I hire a lawn-mowing service in the summer and a snow-shoveling service in the winter. Both providers only accept cash, which is very common for seasonal or independent workers. Because the app forces every transaction to be tied to a digital payment, there’s currently no way to close these entries properly unless I link them to something that doesn’t exist.

Not all transactions in the world will be cashless, and the system shouldn’t assume they are. It would be extremely helpful if the app could allow cash-based entries to be created, recorded, and closed automatically as part of a series without requiring a linked digital payment.

This change would better reflect real-life financial scenarios and make the app much more flexible for users who work with both digital and cash payments.

The envelopes’ balanced rollover each month, but there isn’t a clean feature to allow you to replenish them from your surplus, which feeds into the notion that your left to spend is not real. Having worked in product management and design myself, I get it, you always want to experiment with improvements and users aren’t going to love every change. What I find frustrating about the YNAB app team’s approach is that they keep making major changes to locations of frequently used functions in the app or completely changing user flows with little to no explanation. I find it hard to believe that these changes are improving anyone’s experience with this app. I feel like every time I sort of get used to the current workflow, they redesign it again. This most recent update has tucked a bunch of frequently used functions, like marking transactions as cleared, behind an extra click inside the transaction summary. It is an infuriating extra step and unnecessary friction. Why would you possibly need to make it harder for people to mark their transactions as cleared? That isn’t a destructive process that needs to be hidden. 

I find myself using the app less and less these days and just going back to the website which changes much less often. Maybe that’s the developers’ goal? Who knows. I find it especially frustrating that the experience on the app does not mirror the experience of the UX on the website, and that is probably the biggest sin that these developers have commit committed. As a user, I should be able to seamlessly switch back-and-forth between desktop and Mobile and the UX should be an afterthought. I should not be having to consciously think about and dissect the user flows to re-orient every time I try to use your product. Budgeting is annoying enough as it is, stop trying to reinvent the wheel and just keep the UX consistent. PLEASE.

Useless, confusing updates pushed out constantly that change the layout and functionality. Unfortunately I have to update my YNAB review again. I thought being a beta tester would help shape the direction of the app, but they don’t even send major UI updates to the beta testing pool before shoving them into the official app. In the past 1 year they have pushed several major, confusing updates to the app layout and interface, where each one has changed the location of buttons (right side to left side), the flow of major tasks (opening to a home page instead of the budget), and required more clicks (half of the transaction screen options hidden by a “See More!” tab). Entering a transaction is the backbone of daily use, but has been made more difficult and time consuming. Many changes were obviously flawed in ways that proper beta testing feedback could have prevented (for example, extremely poor color differentiation between future and past transactions), but since user experience isn’t a priority, they ended up rolling back and fixing these issues after they were released to the general user base, causing more updates and layout/color changes that were completely unnecessary. They have not added popular requests such as spending reports that users have requested for over 10 years. There used to be “Four Rules” of the YNAB method, but they quietly removed those and replaced them with gimmicky made-up words such as “spendfulness.” YNAB spent several years building up an online community for users to interact and teach each other, but they just inexplicably fired some of their most popular social media staff and class trainers with 3 hours notice - after sending us an email survey asking how we feel about using AI in our budgets. Apparently there is a new CEO, and I think the shutdown of their main competitor Mint has given them a god complex. All major signs of active ensh*ttification are blinking red, as they destroy all of their community goodwill for the sake of some arbitrary user engagement metrics. It’s the perfect example of the antisocial rot festering within tech companies these days.

YNAB Saved My Financial Future. This is likely going to be a very long review, but for anyone considering a budgeting app change or even just adopting one altogether, this is for you.

6 months ago I woke up and my bank account was drained to 6 cents. Nothing more. My savings had been completely drained by auto-transfers from my checking account over and over until both were empty. I had already racked up a significant amount of credit card debt and had no idea how I would be paying bills that month. I had been reckless with my money, irresponsible…and I knew I needed to change.

So I took a long time researching what I could about finding the right app. I used the Dave Ramsey one for a while (Every dollar) and I used the Experian one for a while, but neither worked. There were limitations on managing the cash flow and carryover and management of actual categories. That is when I landed on YNAB.

I’ll be honest, at first I wasn’t impressed. The app had a lot going on and it took me a lot of time trying to figure out what every button does and what every term means. But for someone with variable income, this app has taught me to manage every new dollar that enters my bank account. I can see in real-time how my money is helping me pay off my debt, and rebuilding my savings. I can monitor what I’m putting towards my retirement accounts and ensuring I have the money when my bi-annual car insurance payments hit. I can plan for a vacation with no stress, because I know that when the money is needed at those times I already have it set aside and not to be touched. The mental and emotional freedom I’ve been given by using a clear and accurate budgeting app has genuinely changed my financial future and my life, and I don’t know if I would have had this much peace without the help of YNAB. 

Their support is also amazing and everything you could ever ask about their app is in their Knowledge Base. I truly have no complaints!

I no longer see income, and even when it was there, it lumped everything together.  Overall, what was a game changer for me just a couple of years ago, is now just cumbersome.

Needless Changes. This app has been really important to me over the last three years, and so I’ve stuck through all the recent UI downgrades that have come since the switch to iOS 26 and the Liquid Glass interface. But today’s update changing the bars for each category into a weird folder with a circle around it feels like a turning point to me. One of the most central parts of the interface is now extremely minimized, and the ability to visually see how much you have spent in a category vs how much you’ve assigned to it is completely gone. I cannot see myself continuing to use this app with this interface, and I’be cancelled my subscription.

Stop making changes with no option to decline them. I don’t care if the team apparently wants to change the entire design and UI philosophy of the app, but having the option to maintain a “Classic”
view or similar should at least be an option. 

The way the budgets look now, the way it hides the budgeted total until you click on the budget line, is horrendous. The little icons on each budget item look busy, and overcomplicate the UI. Why do I want to see “Fully spent” repeated over and over again? Why add so much text to a line when a budget total told me everything I needed to know before?  Entirely removing the ability to see your budget lines at-a-glance is absurd. It feels like an overcorrection towards an ideal that no one but the YNAB team themselves wanted to make. It’s not user friendly, it’s dev friendly. 

I’m capable of rolling with the punches. I’m not one to howl to the heavens when things change. I’m adaptable, and understanding. But 2026 has been an awful year for YNAB updates. All-or-nothing UI updates, no customization to maintain consistency, an entirely useless “Home” page that pushes ads, redundant pages, murdering the design. It feels like kowtowing to a corporate ideal, not ensuring reliable service to users. 

This is an app that people use frequently throughout their daily lives. It is an app for budgeted finances, something that is stressful at a baseline, especially in the world economy today. You have to understand that an unexpected change to someone’s FINANCES is going to be extremely uncomfortable. This is a very personal thing you’re messing with. Why make bracing, irreversible changes with no recourse or options? It’s adding gasoline to a fire. 

Rein it in, guys. I’m glad you’re feeling yourselves and feeling confident, but your design team and philosophy is not more important than a feeling of reliability and comfort for your users. No user thinks about or cares about the vision of YNAB Inc. They want a comfortable place to manage their finances without disruption or surprise. Get over yourselves, be humble.

For example, we want biweekly targets. I’m not going into the details here as YNAB is well aware that customers want this and the subject has been beat to death on reddit and people (including me) have reached out to them directly. I’m specifically referring to how we now have to tap the search box to search the categories list when adding a transaction. This is a daily task that users have built into their muscle memory and now you’re changing it? Why? It’s fine if some people prefer to scroll rather than search. This brings up another area where YNAB is seriously lacking: customization. This isn’t the first time you’ve messed with the categorization workflow, which would suggest that your users are split on whether they like to search or scroll. Here’s an idea: make it a setting! Give us a choice! Stop trying to force a particular way on me! 

Another aspect that has degraded over the years is how we add categories and arrange the order they’re shown in the plan. I want my categories to be in order of when the bills are due. We used to be able to view the due dates for targets while reordering and adding categories but now I have to make sure to figure out where a category goes before I go to the screen to add it. Otherwise I have to leave that screen and return to the plan where I end up tapping on the individual categories and tapping “details” to check due dates, carefully figure out where a new category should live, return to the category add screen and tap “reorder” where I finally move it to its home. 

I guess I just want more customization. As it stands now, if another app were to offer YNAB any competition, I would happily jump ship.

Worth the learning curve. I was BAD with money. Now I’m on top of it and setting/achieving savings goals all thanks to the way YNAB makes you think about money. You have granular clarity of all of your expenses and can customize categories and goals to your needs. Now, there was a learning curve. It took me about 4 months, maybe more, before I felt completely clear and on top of it. There are just some things that are confusing and/or you need to realize first. First and foremost: ALWAYS INPUT AN EXPENSE YOURSELF AT THE TIME OF THAT EXPENSE - waiting for the expense to show up automatically later will wind up screwing up your balances and budget - their automatic import system is not always perfect and can be very delayed, causing your budget to get out of whack if you’re not paying close attentions. And that leads to the second: ALWAYS PAY CLOSE ATTENTION. This is the magic of YNAB. If you are dedicated to leveraging it and learning it, then you will realize that this isn’t about making your financial life easier. Not a “set it and forget it” tool. ITS A TOOL THAT FORCES YOU TO OBTAIN A GRANULAR AND CLEAR VIEW OF YOUR MONEY. To be the master of your money. To help you pay closer attention to it. YNAB is merely a robust, and relatively easy (for what you get) tool to gain this clarity over your finances. You need to learn and be on top of it. And that’s the whole point. There are great YouTube videos out there with tutorials and also videos and seminars on the YNAB site. Plus the customer support has been satisfactory. Last thing I’ll say is, don’t be afraid to start fresh with a budget. To wipe it clean and go again. As I was learning about YNAB, I kept trying to salvage the budget as it got wonky from things that I didn’t properly understand. I started fresh in January with clarity and have been GREAT since. Hope this helps steer some of you to making the leap into YNAB. It’s categorically one of the best financial decisions I’ve ever made.
